correct_citation: Aucejo, E. M., & Romano, T. F. (2014). Assessing the effect of school days and absences on test score performance. CEP Discussion Paper No. 1302, Centre for Economic Performance, LSE (September 2014). Published version: Economics of Education Review 55 (2016), 70-87.
design: Longitudinal administrative panel with student, teacher and school fixed effects (triple FE preferred spec); robustness with lagged test scores, family-year FE and flu-data IV for absences
population_location: North Carolina public school students, grades 3-5, 2006-2010 (NCERDC; about 1,000,903 student-year observations)
outcome: Standardized end-of-grade math and reading test scores
effect_as_reported: Table 11: absences x grade 3 = -0.0025 (math), -0.0015 (reading); grade 4 = -0.0054/-0.0030; grade 5 = -0.0088/-0.0042 SD per absence
excerpt: While each additional absence decreases math (reading) scores by 0.25% (0.15%) of a standard deviation in grade 3, by grade 5 each absences has about three times the impact.
note: Numbers match the 2014 discussion paper's Table 11 exactly. The DP abstract gives slightly different headline figures (10 fewer absences: +5.8% math, +3% reading) from the published 2016 abstract (5.5/2.9); Table 11 values in the published article were not checked.

correct_citation: Aucejo, E. M., & Romano, T. F. (2016). Assessing the effect of school days and absences on test score performance. Economics of Education Review, 55, 70-87.
design: Longitudinal administrative panel with fixed effects; robustness checks include flu-data instrument for absences, family-year fixed effects, excused vs unexcused absences, control for disengagement
population_location: North Carolina public school students (administrative data)
outcome: Standardized math and reading test scores
effect_as_reported: 10-day reduction in absences: +5.5 (math) and +2.9 (reading) percent of an SD; 10 extra school days: +1.7 and +0.8
excerpt: A similar reduction in absences would lead to gains of 5.5 in math and 2.9 in reading. We perform a number of robustness checks including utilizing flu data to instrument for absences, family-year fixed effects
note: RePEc record lists the EER 55(C), 70-87 version. The abstract text drops the unit after 5.5 and 2.9 (it reads 'of a standard deviation' for the calendar figures); reading these as percent of an SD is consistent with the 2014 DP abstract (5.8% and 3%).

correct_citation: Gottfried, M. A. (2009). Excused versus unexcused: How student absences in elementary school affect academic achievement. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4).
design: Longitudinal multilevel administrative data; fixed effects model with classroom-level clustering
population_location: All second- through fourth-grade students, School District of Philadelphia, 1994-2000
outcome: Standardized reading and math test performance
effect_as_reported: Direction only in abstract: higher proportion of excused absences positively related to scores; higher proportion of unexcused absences places students at academic risk, particularly math
excerpt: students with a higher proportion of unexcused absences places them at academic risk, particularly in math achievement and as early as in elementary school.
note: Verified from ERIC abstract only; abstract says 'fixed effects' without specifying student fixed effects, and reports no magnitudes. Volume/issue and pages not confirmed from fetched text.

correct_citation: Balfanz, R., Herzog, L., & Mac Iver, D. J. (2007). Preventing student disengagement and keeping students on the graduation path in urban middle-grades schools: Early identification and effective interventions. Educational Psychologist, 42(4), 223-235.
design: Longitudinal cohort (1996-2004) with multivariate logistic regression; each flag controls for the other flags and race; no control for prior achievement in the graduation model (5th-grade test scores examined separately as weak predictors)
population_location: 12,972 Philadelphia sixth graders (1996 cohort) followed to one year past on-time graduation
outcome: On-time or one-year-late graduation from the school district
effect_as_reported: Chronic absentees (attend <=80%) 68% less likely to graduate; unsatisfactory behavior 56%; failed math 54%; failed English 42%; each p < .0001
excerpt: chronic absentees were 68% less likely than other students to graduate, those with an unsatisfactory behavior grade were 56% less likely to graduate than others, those who failed math were 54% less likely to graduate
note: Matches claim. 'Less likely' figures are from logistic models controlling for other flags and race; the article does not state whether these are odds or probability reductions in that passage.

correct_citation: Allensworth, E. M., & Easton, J. Q. (2007). What matters for staying on-track and graduating in Chicago Public High Schools: A close look at course grades, failures, and attendance in the freshman year. Chicago: Consortium on Chicago School Research, University of Chicago.
design: Longitudinal cohort analysis of administrative records (predictive/descriptive, variance explained); no causal design
population_location: Chicago Public Schools students entering high school (2000-01 cohort for graduation analyses; 2004-05 entering class for course failure)
effect_as_reported: On-track, GPA and semester failures each identify graduates/nongraduates about 80% of the time; background and prior achievement explain about 12% of graduation variation vs 39% for freshman GPA and Fs; freshman absences slightly less predictive
excerpt: all of these factors together explain only about 12 percent of the variation in graduation rates ... students' freshman-year GPA and number of Fs explain 39 percent of the variation in graduation rates.
note: The 12% factors listed include test scores and age at entry plus gender, race and economic status. Adding background and prior achievement to freshman Fs/GPA improves prediction by only about half a percentage point.

correct_citation: Mac Iver, M. A., & Messel, M. (2013). The ABCs of keeping on track to graduation: Research findings from Baltimore. Journal of Education for Students Placed at Risk, 18(1).
design: Longitudinal administrative cohort data; sequentially estimated logistic regression HLM models (multivariate); multinomial models for college outcomes include GPA and 8th-grade test scores
population_location: All first-time 2004-05 and 2005-06 ninth graders, Baltimore City public schools
outcome: On-time graduation (and 1 year past); college enrollment categories
effect_as_reported: Direction only in abstract: 9th-grade attendance and course failure strongest predictors of graduation; gender still significant
excerpt: Sequentially estimated logistic regression hierarchical linear modeling models indicated the strongest predictors of graduation were 9th-grade attendance and course failure, although gender was still significant.
note: Verified from ERIC abstract only; abstract does not say whether the graduation models control for 8th-grade test scores (it names them only for the college-enrollment models). Page range not confirmed from fetched text.

correct_citation: Neild, R. C., Stoner-Eby, S., & Furstenberg, F. (2008). Connecting entrance and departure: The transition to ninth grade and high school dropout. Education and Urban Society, 40(5).

population_location: Cohort of Philadelphia public school students

excerpt: ninth-grade academic outcomes are not simply proxies for student characteristics measured during the pre-high school years and that ninth-grade outcomes add substantially to the ability to predict dropout.
note: Verified from ERIC abstract only. Volume/issue and pages not confirmed from fetched text.

correct_citation: Liu, J., Lee, M., & Gershenson, S. (2021). The short- and long-run impacts of secondary school absences. Journal of Public Economics, 199, 104441. (EdWorkingPaper No. 19-125, Annenberg Institute, Brown University.)
design: Test-score and grade effects: within-student, between-subject variation in class-specific absences (student-year fixed effects). Attainment effects: selection-on-observables regressions with school-by-year and neighborhood-by-year FE and lagged test scores and grades
population_location: Middle and high school students in a large urban school district in California (administrative data with date and class period of each absence)
outcome: State math and ELA test scores, course grades, on-time graduation, college enrollment
effect_as_reported: 10 class absences: -3 to -4% SD test scores, -17 to -18% SD course grades; 10 ninth-grade absences: about 1 to 1.3 percentage points (about 2%) lower graduation and college enrollment
excerpt: ten absences in ninth grade reduce all five measures of educational attainment by about one percentage point, or 2%, and that these effects are statistically significant.
note: Claim overstates the graduation effect: it is about 1-1.3 percentage points, equal to about 2% in relative terms, not 2 percentage points. Also the attainment estimate does not use within-student between-subject variation; it uses selection-on-observables with lagged achievement controls. Test-score figure is correct.

correct_citation: Wang, M.-T., & Fredricks, J. A. (2014). The reciprocal links between school engagement, youth problem behaviors, and school dropout during adolescence. Child Development, 85(2), 722-737.
design: Longitudinal (four waves, grades 7, 9, 11 and one year post high school); latent growth models and autoregressive cross-lagged panel models; covariates include GPA from grades 7-11, SES, demographics, teacher and parent support, school characteristics
population_location: 1,272 youth from 23 public schools in an ethnically and economically diverse East Coast US county (58% African American, 36% European American); 90 dropouts (7.08%)
outcome: School dropout (no diploma, no GED, not enrolled one year after expected graduation)
effect_as_reported: Grade-11 behavioral and emotional engagement negatively related to dropout, behavioral more predictive; cognitive engagement not related; standardized paths in figures not extracted
excerpt: adolescents' academic achievement as well as behavioral and emotional engagement in 11 th grade was negatively related to dropout ... with behavioral engagement being more predictive of dropout than emotional engagement.
note: Behavioral engagement items: homework done, active participation, paying attention, matching the claim. GPA enters as a covariate, not a prior-baseline adjustment of dropout itself.

correct_citation: Fall, A.-M., & Roberts, G. (2012). High school dropouts: Interactions between social context, self-perceptions, school engagement, and student dropout. Journal of Adolescence, 35(4), 787-798.
design: Longitudinal national survey (ELS:2002-2004); structural equation model with 10th-grade engagement and achievement predicting 12th-grade dropout; achievement is concurrent (10th grade), not a prior baseline
population_location: Nationally representative US cohort of 10th graders (ELS:2002; 752 schools, 15,362 base-year students)
outcome: Dropout status in spring of 12th grade (2004)
effect_as_reported: Behavioral engagement beta = -.30, academic engagement beta = -.27, achievement beta = -.20 on dropout (all p < .05)
excerpt: Behavioral and academic engagement and achievement were associated with decreased likelihood of dropping out of high school ( β = −.30, p < .05, β = −.27, p < .05, and β = −.20, p < .05, respectively).
note: Academic engagement is teacher-reported (English and math teachers' ratings of effort, persistence, attention); behavioral engagement is student-reported (not skipping school, not getting in trouble), so 'teacher-rated' applies only to academic engagement.
